explanations: luna: The section develops weak lightning at cloud edges; this rainstorm parable explicitly stages rain from the sky, darkness, thunder, and lightning, though its primary point is people in doubt. | terra: A rain cloud contains darkness, thunder, and lightning, supplying a direct Quranic storm setting for the section's first cloud and its marginal flash.

luna: The verse's برق nearly snatches sight: it gives the section's faint cloud-edge flash a brighter storm counterpart and makes visibility itself unstable. | terra: The lightning nearly snatches sight, yet people walk when it lights and stop when darkness returns; this turns watching intermittent nocturnal light into movement and contrasts with the lexicon's weak lightning watched through the night.

luna: The section's lexical image of the sky as what covers above extends downward through cloud and rain to pasture; this verse joins the sky as a canopy, water sent down, and fruit brought out from earth. | terra: Earth is made a resting place, sky a canopy, water descends, and fruits are brought out as provision; it renders the section's sky-to-earth vertical column in one ayah.
terra: Clouds shade the people from above, directly exemplifying the section's definition of sky as whatever rises over and shades a person, though no rain falls here.

luna: This sign sequence places winds, clouds held between sky and earth, rain, and revived land together, matching the section's vertical passage from cloud to living growth. | terra: Water from the sky revives earth after death, creatures spread, winds turn, and clouds are controlled between sky and earth; the ayah lays out the section's complete vertical and moving weather system.

luna: The verse's seed yields seven ears, a specific image of growth multiplying from what is sown; this adds a crop-growth parallel to the section's plant emerging from earth, though its point is charitable giving.
terra: A downpour strikes thin soil on rock and leaves it bare, reversing the section's first rain that marks earth with vegetation.

luna: The verse pictures a fertile garden on a height receiving heavy rain or drizzle and yielding fruit, a specific soil-and-rain counterpart to the section's pasture emerging under rain. | terra: A garden on high ground bears doubled produce under heavy rain and still yields under light rain, showing how differing rain intensities nourish rather than merely accompany the green mark.

luna: The verse's flourishing garden is struck by a fiery whirlwind and burned; this is a concrete reversal of the section's rain-fed green growth, though the cause is sudden fire rather than natural drying. | terra: A lush garden of palms, vines, fruits, and rivers is struck by a fiery whirlwind and burned when its owner is vulnerable, sharply reversing sustained green provision into sudden ruin.

luna: The verse lists crops and livestock among the adornments of worldly life, a concrete link between the section's pasture imagery and its contrast with what lasts. | terra: Livestock and cultivated fields appear among the adorned desires of worldly life, joining the pasture's animal-and-plant world to the lower life's attraction.
terra: A bitterly cold wind strikes and destroys a crop, setting destructive weather against the cloud and rain that nourish pasture.

terra: Abundant rain and flowing rivers accompany the establishment of earlier generations before those generations are destroyed, placing heavenly provision and human transience in one historical cycle.
terra: God knows the falling leaf, the grain hidden in earth's darkness, and every moist and dry thing; hiddenness, plant location, and the wet-to-dry poles of the image meet under divine knowledge.
terra: God splits grain and seed-stone and brings living from dead and dead from living, expressing both concrete plant emergence and the reversible life/death relation behind the pasture.

luna: The verse moves from water sent down to varied plants, green growth, grain, dates, and ripening fruit, a close Qur'anic staging of rain bringing vegetation out. | terra: Water descends from the sky and God brings out every kind of growth, including خَضِرًا from which grain emerges, making green life the explicit product of the omitted rain.
terra: Gardens, palms, and crops of differing produce are followed by the command to eat at fruiting and give their due at harvest, extending the section's plant lifetime into ripening and reaping.

luna: The passage sends winds before mercy, carries heavy clouds to a dead land, sends rain, brings out fruit, and compares this to bringing out the dead; it gathers the section's full rain-to-growth-to-resurrection chain. | terra: The winds herald mercy, heavy clouds are driven to dead land, water descends, fruits are brought out, and the dead are likewise brought out; this supplies the rain omitted between 87:4 and 87:5 and joins خ ر ج to resurrection and remembrance.

luna: The section defines المرعى as plant, place, and grazing; this adjacent verse says good land yields its vegetation by its Lord's permission, while poor land yields little. | terra: The good land brings forth its growth بِإِذْنِ رَبِّهِ while bad land yields only scant growth; following 7:57, it connects Rabb, emergence, and the section's patch-by-patch difference in soil.
terra: Salih's she-camel is to be left to eat on God's earth, repeating the animal-side realization of pasture as grazing.
terra: The cloud again shades a people, repeating the overhead-covering sense developed from س م و while the surrounding passage supplies water and food by other means.
terra: The addressees are asked whether they are content with worldly life instead of the Hereafter and are told its enjoyment is slight, closely restating 87:16–17 without the plant simile.

luna: The verse makes worldly life a rain-fed crop that flourishes, then is harvested away as if it had not flourished yesterday, sharpening the section's green-to-debris arc. | terra: Rain makes the earth's vegetation mingle and adorn the land before it is made harvested as though it had not flourished yesterday; the sudden فَجَعَلْنَٰهَا transition expands 87:5's compressed ending.
terra: The sky is promised as abundant rain that adds strength, presenting rain as sustained divine provision rather than naming the vegetation it produces.
terra: The she-camel is to be left to eat on God's earth, a concrete animal-side realization of المرعى as grazing, though the verse does not show the grass's growth.

terra: The king sees seven green ears of grain and others dry, holding fresh and desiccated plant states together just as the section reads both lush darkness and blackened waste through one color image.
terra: The same green and dry ears are repeated when Joseph is asked for their meaning, preserving the explicit juxtaposition of a plant's two ends in the interpretive scene.
luna: This preceding verse spreads the earth and names rivers and paired fruits; it supplies the earth-and-fruit setting continued by 13:4's gardens and crops.

luna: The verse contrasts gardens, crops, and date palms watered by one water but yielding differently, a specific parallel to the section's patchy first growth and varied pasture. | terra: Adjacent plots, gardens, crops, and palms receive one water yet differ in produce, a Quranic counterpart to the section's patchy earth whose growth appears in one place and not another.

luna: The section's root خ ف ي is given a weak-flash sense at cloud edges; this verse explicitly joins lightning that evokes fear and hope to heavy clouds. | terra: Lightning brings fear and hope while heavy clouds are raised, directly joining the flash to the laden cloud and showing a more forceful manifestation than the section's faint one.
terra: Thunder glorifies God with praise while angels do so in awe and thunderbolts are sent; the storm scene itself performs the glorification commanded at the image's opening.

luna: The section's غثاء is flood-carried vegetation piled together; here floodwater carries زبدًا that passes away while what benefits people remains, joining torrent residue to the distinction between passing and lasting. | terra: Water descends, valleys flow according to measure, and the torrent carries swelling foam which vanishes while what benefits people remains; this is the section's flood-borne غثاء read through the boundary between what passes and what stays.
terra: The promised garden has enduring fruit and shade, the precise vegetal opposite of pasture whose taste, greenness, and body are carried away.
terra: Death comes to the punished person from every side وَمَا هُوَ بِمَيِّتٍ, another precise boundary between ordinary dying matter and the person who cannot complete death.

luna: The good word is compared to a good tree with firm roots and branches reaching skyward, joining the section's rooted emergence to its vertical sky-to-pasture image. | terra: The good word is a good tree with firm root and branch in the sky, answering the section's short-lived grass with stability across the same earth-to-sky axis.

luna: The tree yields fruit by its Lord's permission; this gives a recurring, sustained counterpart to the section's pasture and its root-family image of a cloud that nurtures plants. | terra: The tree gives fruit in every season بِإِذْنِ رَبِّهَا, directly opposing the summer-withering pasture and bringing Rabb into enduring growth.

luna: The bad word is compared to a tree uprooted from the earth with no stability, a specific plant reversal beside the section's growth from soil and its later debris. | terra: The bad word is an uprooted tree with no stability, marking the boundary on the other side of the enduring tree and resembling vegetation reduced to unattached debris.

luna: The verse sends water from heaven and brings out fruits as provision, a direct rain-to-harvest formulation alongside the section's pasture. | terra: Water descends from the sky and fruits are brought out as provision, restating the core vertical movement from above to emerged food.
terra: Earth is spread and every measured thing is caused to grow in it, joining vegetation to the section's preceding idea of divine measure.
terra: All things have their treasuries with God and descend only in known measure, framing the rain in 15:22 as hidden, measured provision.

luna: The section names a southern wind that sustains and drives clouds; this verse gives winds a concrete role in pollination and then connects them to water sent down. | terra: Fertilizing winds are sent, water descends from the sky, and people are not its storekeepers, directly linking moving air, rain, life, and provision beyond human control.
terra: Livestock are beautiful when brought home and when sent out to pasture, supplying the daily herd movement implicit in المرعى's grazing sense.

luna: This verse says rainwater gives drink and produces vegetation for grazing, directly linking rain to pasture and animal feeding. | terra: Water descends for drink and grows trees فِيهِ تُسِيمُونَ, where livestock are sent to graze; rain, plant, pasture, and the act of grazing meet in one verse.

luna: The verse names crops, olives, palms, grapes, and fruits grown by the rain, widening the same provision scene from pasture to harvest. | terra: With that water God grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and every fruit, continuing 16:10's rain-to-grazing scene into the abundance hidden between 87:4 and 87:5.
terra: The varied colors of what God has multiplied on earth provide a wider palette for the section's attention to green, yellow, and black plant states.

luna: The verse says God revives the earth after its death with rain; it gives Qur'anic form to the section's plant journey from dead soil to living growth. | terra: Water from the sky gives earth life after its death, stating the life-giving role that explains why the section's lexicon can call rain “life.”

luna: The section sets the plant's short life beside what is better and more abiding; this verse says what people have runs out while what is with God remains. | terra: What people possess runs out while مَا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ بَاقٍ, stating in abstract terms the same passing-versus-remaining boundary shown by grass and enduring good.
terra: Earth's contents are made an adornment and a test, giving the flourishing first half of the image whose removal follows in 18:8.
terra: Earth's adornment is destined to become barren ground, a direct large-scale counterpart to green pasture becoming lifeless refuse.
luna: The garden story named immediately before the section's worldly-life parable begins with two gardens of vines, palms, and crops, the lush cultivated scene that the next image makes transient.
luna: The verse says both gardens yield their produce and a river runs between them, supplying the abundance that makes the later collapse meaningful.
luna: The owner enters his garden while wronging himself and says he does not think it will ever perish; the section's plant cycle directly overturns that confidence.
luna: The garden owner doubts the Hour and his return to his Lord, making the section's temporary vegetation and lasting Hereafter distinction especially pointed.
luna: The companion warns that a calamity from heaven could strike the garden and leave it bare and slippery, a destructive reversal of rain-fed flourishing.
luna: The warning that the garden's water may sink away supplies the opposite boundary to the section's rain that makes pasture emerge.
luna: The garden's produce is destroyed and its owner wrings his hands over what he spent; this is a concrete human loss beside the section's natural conversion of green growth to debris.

luna: The verse explicitly compares worldly life to rain from heaven: earth's growth becomes dry fragments scattered by winds, almost exactly the section's plant-to-debris sequence. | terra: The world's life is rain from the sky, mingled vegetation, and finally هَشِيمًا scattered by winds, giving the full Quranic analogue of pasture becoming dry debris.

luna: The section links أبقى to what endures; this verse names the lasting good deeds as better with one's Lord than the rain-grown life that vanishes. | terra: وَٱلْبَٰقِيَٰتُ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتُ names the enduring counterweight immediately after 18:45's scattered plants, linking the section's ب ق ي family to its fading worldly grass.

luna: The source section uses the root خ ف ي for lightning that glimmers faintly at a cloud's edge; this verse uses أَخْفَى for what is more concealed, a lexical boundary between faintly seen and hidden. | terra: God knows the secret and what is still more hidden, closely paralleling 87:7's divine knowledge and anchoring خ ف ي in concealment before the section explores its faint-lightning and rain-expulsion senses.

terra: Moses sees a distant fire at night and asks his family to remain while he seeks a brand or guidance; this may echo the section's lexical night-watcher scanning for lightning, though the light is fire rather than lightning.
terra: The Hour is said to be nearly concealed, a primary concealment use of خ ف ي that helps mark the semantic distance to the section's weak flash at a cloud edge.

luna: This is Pharaoh's question, “Who is your Lord, Moses?”; the section cites it to frame Moses' answer about the Lord who creates, guides, and brings forth plants in 20:50 and 20:53. | terra: Pharaoh's question “Who is your Lord, Moses?” makes the رب in 20:50's creation-and-guidance answer an explicit point of dispute.

luna: The answer names the Lord as the one who gives each thing its form and then guides it, joining the section's Lord-language to the ordered emergence of pasture. | terra: Moses identifies “our Lord” as the one who gave each thing its creation and then guided it, repeating the creation-and-guidance order that precedes the pasture in surah 87.

terra: Moses says knowledge of former generations is with his Lord in a record and that his Lord neither errs nor forgets, joining Rabb, hidden knowledge, and the no-forgetting context near the quoted Moses passage.

luna: The verse describes earth spread out, water sent down, and varied plants brought forth; the source section's root خ ر ج for extracting vegetation is explicit here. | terra: Water descends from the sky and أَخْرَجْنَا بِهِۦٓ diverse pairs of plants, explicitly filling the section's hidden link from sky to rain to vegetation.

luna: This continuation tells people to eat and pasture their cattle, directly activating the section's threefold sense of المرعى as vegetation, grazing place, and grazing. | terra: “Eat and pasture your livestock” makes plant growth from 20:53 into both human food and the act of grazing, unpacking المرعى's combined senses.

luna: The verse says humans are created from earth, returned to it, and brought out again, extending the plant's earth-to-emergence cycle to resurrection. | terra: Humans are created from earth, returned to it, and brought out from it again, extending the plant emergence of 20:53 into the same resurrection pattern.
terra: The magicians declare God better and more lasting after rejecting Pharaoh's temporal coercion, another lived choice of the enduring over the nearer power.

luna: The verse says the condemned person neither dies nor lives in the Fire, the exact boundary the section sets against a plant's living and dead phases. | terra: لَا يَمُوتُ فِيهَا وَلَا يَحْيَىٰ exactly repeats the condition later voiced in 87:13, setting the plant's clear life-and-death cycle against hell's suspended condition.

luna: The verse contrasts worldly enjoyment with provision from one's Lord that is better and أبقى; the source section uses the same root أبقى to frame what outlasts the plant's short life. | terra: The زَهْرَةَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا is temporary display, while the Lord's provision is خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ; the flower image and exact lasting comparison join the grass cycle to 87:16–17.

luna: The verse joins the heavens and earth being separated with every living thing made from water, making water the source of life in the section's rain-and-pasture image. | terra: Every living thing is made from water, supporting the lexical claim that rain is called “life,” although this ayah speaks of water generally rather than pasture.
terra: A people's sheep graze through a cultivated field at night, realizing grazing as an action while showing it as damage to another person's growth.

luna: The barren earth receives water, stirs, swells, and grows varied plants; the verse then compares this revival to human resurrection. | terra: Barren earth receives water, then ٱهْتَزَّتْ وَرَبَتْ and grows beautiful pairs; its quivering growth directly matches the section's lexical definition of a living plant and makes that revival an argument for resurrection.

luna: The verse says rain from the sky makes the earth green, a direct compact formulation of the section's cloud-to-rain-to-pasture scene. | terra: Water descends and the earth becomes مُخْضَرَّةً, giving the immediate green mark left on soil by the first rain.

luna: This verse sends down water from the sky in measure and settles it in the earth, while warning that it could be taken away; it frames the rain on which pasture depends. | terra: Water descends from the sky بِقَدَرٍ and is lodged in the earth, joining measured provision to its hidden storage and to the possibility that God can remove it.

luna: This continuation brings forth gardens of dates and grapes and other fruits, a specific harvest following the measured water. | terra: Gardens and abundant fruits are produced by the measured, stored water of 23:18, completing its descent-to-growth sequence.

luna: This next verse adds the olive tree of Mount Sinai, yielding oil and food, to the date, grape, and garden produce named in 23:19. | terra: The tree from Sinai grows bearing oil and food, continuing the measured rain and gardens of 23:18–19 with a particular nourishing plant.

luna: The source section defines غثاء as plant gathered and carried by a flood; this verse uses غثاء for a people after the cry, transferring the plant's debris image to a community. | terra: فَجَعَلْنَٰهُمْ غُثَآءً repeats both the transformation verb and غثاء but makes a destroyed people, rather than pasture, the flood-like refuse.

luna: The verse describes clouds joined and piled into layers, rain emerging through them, and lightning; it supplies the cloud-and-flash scene developed by the section. | terra: Clouds are driven, joined, and heaped; rain and hail emerge from them, and their lightning nearly takes sight, staging the whole cloud-to-rain movement while contrasting with the section's weak crosswise flash.
terra: God creates everything and determines it with exact measure, paralleling the creation-and-measure order that frames the pasture image without itself naming vegetation.

luna: This verse sends winds as heralds before mercy and sends down purifying water from the sky, matching the section's wind, cloud, and rain sequence. | terra: Winds are sent as heralds before mercy and pure water descends from the sky, repeating the cloud system that supplies the missing rain.

luna: The water revives a dead land and gives drink to people and animals; its life-giving rain stands against the section's later dry debris. | terra: That water revives dead land and gives drink to cattle and people, linking the rain called life to creatures sustained by it.
terra: The command to look at earth and how many noble pairs God has caused to grow directs attention to the same visible act of pasture emerging.

luna: The word نُرَبِّكَ is from the source section's root ر ب ب in the explicit nurturing sense: Pharaoh says he raised Moses as a child. The section links that root-family to a cloud that nurtures plants, extending the sustaining image to human upbringing.
terra: Abraham names his Lord as the one who created him and guides him, repeating the creation-then-guidance sequence that frames the pasture image.
terra: The same Lord feeds and gives drink, turning creation and guidance in 26:78 toward the nourishment supplied by pasture and rain.
terra: The same Lord causes death and then gives life, stating in personal terms the complete transition that the section watches in soil and grass.
terra: The punishment of the Day of the Canopy turns an overhead cloud-like shade from shelter and promised rain into destruction.
terra: Moses' sight of a distant fire and hope for news or a burning brand is a plausible nonlexical parallel to watching a remote nocturnal flash, but the ayah does not involve cloud or rain.

luna: The verse asks who sends water down and brings forth gardens, then says people cannot make their trees grow; it makes vegetation's emergence a sign of the Lord's agency. | terra: The Creator sends water from the sky and grows flourishing gardens that humans could not grow, reinforcing the divine subject behind pasture's emergence.
terra: The crowd watering flocks and the two women holding theirs back place herd, herders, and water together, a social counterpart to pasture's grass-place-grazing complex.

terra: Moses sees fire from the side of the mountain while traveling at night and goes toward it for news or warmth; the connection is limited to the section's secondary scene of sustained attention to light in darkness.

luna: The verse calls worldly gifts adornment and says what is with God is better and more abiding, echoing the section's contrast between temporary green growth and what remains. | terra: Worldly enjoyment and adornment are set against what is with God as better and more lasting, stating the same comparison the fading pasture makes visible.

luna: The verse joins rain from the sky to earth revived after death, then asks who does this; it is a direct formulation of the section's rain-to-life pattern. | terra: Water from the sky revives earth after death, and the expected confession that God did it preserves the divine agency central to 87:4.
luna: The verse says the living comes from the dead and the dead from the living, and that earth is revived after death, directly stating the cycle the section makes visible in pasture.

luna: The verse links lightning that raises fear and hope to rain and earth revived after death, combining the section's faint flash with its rain-grown vegetation. | terra: Lightning is shown for fear and hope, water descends from the sky, and earth is revived after death, uniting the section's faint cloud-edge flash with the rain called life.

luna: This verse says that when God calls people from the earth they come forth; the source section's root خ ر ج describes pasture brought out from earth, and here the same extraction image points to resurrection.
luna: This verse calls winds glad tidings of mercy and of ships seeking provision; it prepares the cloud-and-rain action in 30:48 that the section's image develops.

luna: The verse says winds drive clouds, which spread and pile up, then rain emerges; this directly stages the section's cloud being carried to the land. | terra: Winds raise clouds, God spreads or fragments them, and rain is seen emerging from within, closely staging the section's first appearing and lingering cloud.
luna: This verse describes people's despair before rain arrives; the following 30:50 turns to the traces of mercy and revived earth, completing the weather reversal.

luna: The command to look at the traces of God's mercy points to the earth revived after death; this matches the source section's first-rain mark on the land and its green return. | terra: The reader is told to look at the effects of divine mercy in earth's revival after death and infer the revival of the dead, exactly the interpretive move made from living grass.

luna: After 30:50 describes revived earth, this verse presents a wind and something seen yellow; it gives the rain-revived scene its specific yellowing reversal. | terra: A sent wind makes the crop yellow and people become ungrateful, reversing the life-bearing wind and rain of 30:48–50.

luna: The verse joins rain sent down from the sky to the growth of every noble kind of plant, a compact version of the section's vertical rain-to-pasture column. | terra: Water from the sky causes every noble kind to grow, another direct statement of the rain-to-emergence link compressed out of 87:4.

luna: The verse drives water to barren land and brings out crops eaten by people and their grazing animals, directly joining soil, rain, and pasture. | terra: Water is driven to barren land and brings out crops eaten by livestock and people, directly uniting the moving cloud-water system with pasture and provision.
terra: Two fertile gardens and the command to eat the Lord's provision display the sweet, nourished state before the flood reversal in 34:16.
terra: The dam flood replaces two fruitful gardens with bitter fruit and sparse trees, combining destructive water, lost sweetness, and ruined vegetation.

luna: The verse describes winds driving clouds to dead land and reviving earth after its death, then names resurrection; it closely parallels the section's weather and plant cycle. | terra: Winds raise clouds, clouds are driven to dead land, and earth is revived; كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلنُّشُورُ makes the exact cloud-rain-life movement a resurrection sign.

luna: The verse says water from the sky brings fruits of varied colors; this gives a Qur'anic color counterpart to the section's dark-green-to-black description of أَحْوَى. | terra: Water from the sky brings fruits of varied colors, followed by white, red, and intensely black mountain tracts; it places rain-grown color beside the section's black-over-white خ ر ج color sense.
terra: People, creatures, and livestock have varied colors, extending 35:27's black, white, and red landscape colors to animals and recalling the section's camel-color definition of أَحْوَىٰ.
terra: The people of the Fire are not finished by death and their punishment is not lightened, extending the boundary expressed by “neither dies nor lives.”

luna: The dead earth is a sign: God revives it and brings grain from it for food, matching the section's emergence of pasture from soil. | terra: A sign is the dead earth: God gives it life and brings grain out of it, compressing death, revival, and concrete emergence into one agricultural scene.

luna: This continuation places date palms and grape gardens in the revived land, specifying the produce that follows the grain. | terra: Gardens of palms and grapes and flowing springs continue 36:33's revived dead earth, showing the abundant living form reached after grain is brought out.
luna: The verse asks whether people made these gardens grow or God did, tying the crop scene to the section's Lord as giver and grower.
luna: The verse answers who can revive decayed bones: the one who created them first. Its contribution is the resurrection claim, followed in 36:80 by a green-tree-and-fire sign.

luna: The verse asks who made the tree from which people kindle fire; green vegetation thus yields fire, joining the section's pasture cycle to the later Fire image in Surah 87. | terra: Fire is produced from a green tree, making living greenness and burning meet at a boundary that sharpens the section's later fire/life opposition.

luna: The verse sends water down, brings out crops of varied colors, then turns them yellow and into debris; جَعَلَهُ in the source section likewise names the plant's change of state, and this verse ends with a reminder. | terra: Water descends, runs as springs, brings out plants of varied colors, then the plants wither yellow and are made حُطَامًا; ثُمَّ يَجْعَلُهُۥ and لَذِكْرَىٰ join 87:5's transformation to 87:9's reminder.
terra: Provision is sent down from the sky and only one who turns back remembers, linking unnamed heavenly provision to the section's omitted rain and its movement toward reminder.
terra: Human life is compressed from dust through infancy, maturity, old age, and death, a non-botanical parallel to the whole lifespan compressed into the section's two plant ayat.

luna: The verse points to earth that is subdued, then stirs and grows when water descends; its revival is called a sign of God's power. | terra: Humbled earth quivers and swells when water descends, and its reviver is declared able to revive the dead; this is the same living plant sign and resurrection bridge as the section's journey from dead soil.

luna: The verse sends rain after people have despaired and spreads mercy, a specific reversal from withheld water to renewed life. | terra: Rain descends after despair and mercy is spread, fitting the section's first life-giving rain though the ayah leaves vegetation unstated.
terra: Worldly enjoyment is set against what is with God as better and more lasting, directly stating the value contrast that the section makes visible through transient grass.

luna: The verse sends down water from the sky in due measure, revives a dead town, and says people will be brought out likewise; it joins measured rain to resurrection. | terra: Water descends from the sky in measure, revives a dead land, and is followed by كَذَٰلِكَ تُخْرَجُونَ, joining measured rain to human emergence.

luna: The verse groups night and day, rain that revives earth after death, and winds as signs, bringing together several elements of the section's weather cycle. | terra: Provision descends from the sky, revives earth after death, and is named beside the turning winds, joining sustenance, life, and moving air.

luna: The people mistake an approaching cloud for rain, but it is a painful wind; this reverses the section's life-giving cloud and rain expectation. | terra: A cloud appearing over the valleys is welcomed as rain, but is identified as the hastened punishment bearing a painful wind; first appearance and expected rain are decisively reversed.

luna: The wind destroys everything by its Lord's command, a specific boundary to the section's cloud as the source of pasture and growth. | terra: The wind destroys everything by its Lord's command, showing what a cloud-driven wind can leave when it bears devastation instead of pasture-making rain.

terra: سِيمَاهُمْ marks the believers' faces, and the same ayah compares them to a crop that sends out its shoot, strengthens, and stands firm; it uniquely joins the recorded و س م derivation's mark with visible plant growth.

luna: The verse describes blessed rain, gardens, and grain for harvest, a direct rain-to-food counterpart to the pasture emergence in the section. | terra: Blessed water descends from the sky and produces gardens and harvest grain, presenting rain as the life-bearing provision behind emergence.

luna: This continuation adds tall date palms with layered fruit, showing the rain's yield in a concrete plant form. | terra: Tall palms with layered clusters stand between blessed rain in 50:9 and provision and revival in 50:11, contributing the passage's most visibly upright growth.

luna: The verse says rain revives a dead land and calls resurrection “the خروج”; it explicitly moves from plant revival to the dead being brought out. | terra: The water is provision, revives a dead land, and ends كَذَٰلِكَ ٱلْخُرُوجُ, explicitly turning plant emergence into the pattern of resurrection.
terra: Earth splits from the resurrected as they emerge swiftly, completing the literal human خروج anticipated by the rain-and-revival image at 50:11.
terra: The wind sent to ʿĀd is explicitly barren, the opposite of the fertilizing, rain-bearing air in the section's weather column.
terra: That wind leaves whatever it passes like decayed matter, reaching the same wrecked endpoint as غثاء without the intervening green life.

terra: People seeing a fragment of sky falling call it a piled cloud, a contrary cloud-recognition scene that echoes the first appearance of cloud while exposing refusal to recognize impending destruction.

terra: People emerge from graves like scattered locusts; this may faintly parallel rain forcing hidden creatures from holes and the section's concrete خ ر ج imagery, but neither rain nor mice appears in the ayah.
terra: A violent wind leaves people like uprooted palm trunks, another transfer of ruined vegetation imagery to a destroyed people beside the section's غثاء comparison.
terra: A destroyed people become like dry stalks used by a pen-builder, another transfer of plant wreckage imagery to human ruin comparable to 23:41.
terra: Everything is created according to measure, a concise Quranic parallel to the measured ordering that precedes pasture in surah 87.
luna: The verse says herbs and trees prostrate; alongside Surah 87's opening command to glorify the Most High, it makes vegetation itself part of the worship scene.
luna: This adjacent verse says the heaven was raised and balance set, carrying the sky-and-earth frame of 55:6 into the section's vertical image from above to pasture.
luna: The passage next says the earth was laid out for living creatures, giving the ground beneath the section's emerging pasture its place in the created order.
luna: This continuation names fruit and date palms, extending the earth's produce scene beyond the pasture.
luna: The verse adds grain and fragrant plants, a specific crop-and-herb counterpart to the section's grass and grazing.
terra: Everything upon the earth is perishing, extending the pasture's short life into a universal statement about the earthly scene.
terra: The face of the majestic and generous Lord remains after all earthly things perish, supplying the enduring pole opposite 55:26 and the section's decaying vegetation.

luna: The source section defines أَحْوَى as darkened from green; this verse calls two gardens مُدْهَامَّتَان, a Qur'anic image of greenery so dense it appears dark. | terra: مُدْهَآمَّتَانِ describes two gardens dark with lush green, supplying the living, luxuriant pole that the section says أَحْوَىٰ can hold beside blackened decay.
luna: The two gardens of Paradise have gushing springs, a lasting garden scene that marks a boundary against the section's pasture that dries and is carried away.
luna: This garden passage names fruit, date palms, and pomegranates; it continues the unwithering produce scene begun in 55:64.

luna: After the surah's images of prostrating plants, raised heaven, earth, fruit, and dark gardens, this closing verse blesses the name of the Lord, echoing the section's opening “name of your Lord” across a botanical and celestial sequence.
terra: Abundant fruit in the garden supplies a flourishing vegetal counter-scene to the pasture's quick exhaustion.
terra: The fruit is neither cut off nor withheld, making unending plant provision a specific contrast to grass that dries and is swept away.

luna: The verse asks people to consider what they sow, introducing a crop cycle whose growth the next verse assigns to God. | terra: The question “Have you seen what you sow?” opens a compact sequence about human planting, divine growth, and possible reduction to debris that closely parallels 87:4–5.

luna: The question “Are you the growers, or are We?” makes plant emergence depend on divine agency, as in the section's Lord and pasture. | terra: The ayah asks whether people make the crop grow or God does, making the divine agency behind “He brought out the pasture” explicit.

luna: The verse says God could make the crop حُطَامًا; the source section's غثاء is the flood-gathered dry plant residue, a close parallel in the crop's broken end. | terra: God could make the crop حُطَامًا, directly matching the pasture's divinely caused conversion into dry wreckage.
luna: The following lament says the crop leaves them in debt, showing the human loss after the possible crop failure in 56:65.
luna: This continuation says they have been deprived, completing the crop-failure outcome that contrasts with pasture as provision.

luna: The verse asks who sends down drinking water from rainclouds, returning directly to the water source of the section's vegetation. | terra: The sequence turns from crop to the water people drink, bringing the otherwise omitted water into the same act of contemplating provision.

luna: The verse asks whether people or God send the rainwater, underscoring the giver behind the section's rain-fed growth. | terra: The question asks whether people sent water down from ٱلْمُزْنِ, the rain clouds, or God did, naming the cloud source that the section reconstructs behind the pasture.

luna: The verse says God could make the water bitter; this is a specific reversal of rain as life-giving water. | terra: God could make the rain-cloud water bitter, a boundary that answers both drinkable rain and the section's pasture losing its sweetness.
luna: The verse asks people to consider the fire they kindle; it opens the adjacent creation passage in which 56:72 identifies the tree from which fire is made.
luna: The verse asks who made the tree that supplies kindling; it specifically joins plant growth to fire, a reversal of the section's green pasture and a bridge to Surah 87's Fire.
luna: The continuation calls that fire a reminder and provision for travelers, joining the tree-to-fire image to the section's movement from the plant cycle toward reminder.
terra: فَسَبِّحْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلْعَظِيمِ concludes the sowing, rain-cloud, and water sequence with the same command to glorify the Lord's name that opens surah 87.
terra: فَسَبِّحْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلْعَظِيمِ repeats the command-object formula of 87:1 and helps keep “name” and “Lord” as their primary meanings beneath the section's family imagery.

luna: The verse says God gives life to earth after its death and makes the signs clear, a concise statement of the section's dead-soil-to-green motif. | terra: God's reviving of earth after its death is itself an explained sign, the same perceptible transition the section sees in fresh moving plants.

luna: The verse makes worldly life a rain-fed crop that grows, yellows, and becomes حُطَامًا; it explicitly frames the plant's decay as a reminder of passing life. | terra: Worldly life is vegetation after rain that delights growers, then يَهِيجُ, yellows, and becomes حُطَامًا; the verse directly stages the green-to-dry journey used to expose the lower life's brevity.
terra: If water sinks away, no one can bring flowing water back; this makes the normally hidden provision perceptible through its possible withdrawal.

luna: The source section gives اسم an attested alternative derivation from وسم and pictures first rain marking earth with plants; this verse uses سَنَسِمُهُ for branding a person, a distant but concrete mark-image rather than a shared root identity. | terra: سَنَسِمُهُ عَلَى ٱلْخُرْطُومِ uses branding as punitive exposure, contrasting with the recorded و س م derivation in which first rain marks earth by making green growth visible.
terra: A visitation circles the garden while its owners sleep, supplying the unseen cause for the blackened or stripped result stated in 68:20.
terra: The garden becomes like a stripped or blackened field overnight, a sudden dark endpoint that illuminates أَحْوَىٰ as decayed blackness rather than lush dark green.
terra: After the relentless wind, people lie like hollow fallen palm trunks, repeating the image of human destruction as plant wreckage.
terra: The same command to glorify the name of the Magnificent Lord closes another surah, confirming the worship formula echoed at 87:1.
terra: The sky is promised as abundant rain, using the upper covering itself as the source of the water developed in the section's س م و family.
terra: That rain supplies wealth, children, gardens, and rivers, completing its role as sustained provision and growth.
luna: The verse says God caused people to grow from earth like a plant, giving the section's plant emergence a direct human counterpart.
luna: This continuation says people return to earth and are brought out again, completing the human cycle beside 71:17's growth from earth.
terra: “You love the immediate life” repeats the human preference voiced in 87:16, while the section's plant cycle shows why that preference is misplaced.
terra: “You leave the Hereafter” supplies the neglected counterpart to 75:20, matching the section's turn from the lower life to what is better and more lasting.
terra: People love the immediate life and leave a weighty day behind them, another direct formulation of the stance that the pasture's rapid decay exposes.
terra: Sweet water is given to drink, a direct positive pole for the section's mention of sweetness lost when floodwater turns pasture into debris.

terra: One received image compares the fire's sparks to yellow camels; it may recall the section's secondary definition of an أَحْوَىٰ camel as carrying yellow with darker color, but the word is also understood through a rope-like image and no pasture appears.

luna: The verse says abundant rain is sent from clouds, followed by grain and gardens in 78:15–16; it is another compact rain-to-harvest scene. | terra: Profuse water descends from rain clouds, naming the cloud-to-rain step developed in the section.

luna: This adjacent verse names grain and vegetation brought forth by the abundant rain in 78:14. | terra: Grain and vegetation are brought out by that rain, supplying the next link in the vertical chain.

luna: The following verse adds lush gardens to the grain and vegetation sequence begun in 78:14. | terra: Dense gardens complete the rain sequence with dark abundance, the living visual pole opposite the later black refuse.
terra: Pharaoh's “I am your lord, the most high” usurps the exact رب/أعلى relation of 87:1, clarifying by reversal whose name the command to glorify bears.

luna: The verse says God brought out the earth's water and pasture; the source section's مرعى carries vegetation, pasture-place, and grazing, all concentrated here. | terra: أَخْرَجَ مِنْهَا مَآءَهَا وَمَرْعَىٰهَا places water and pasture in the same act of emergence and is the Quran's closest verbal counterpart to 87:4.

luna: This verse says the water, pasture, and mountains are provision for people and their livestock, completing the pasture's role as sustenance. | terra: Water and pasture in 79:31 are declared provision for people and livestock, spelling out the feeding relation contained in المرعى.

luna: The command to consider food introduces the sequence in 80:25–32, where rain, split earth, grain, fruit, pasture, and provision explain what sustains life. | terra: The command that a person look at their food establishes the contemplative stance for the rain, cracked earth, vegetation, and pasture that follow.

luna: The verse says water is poured down, giving the rain source for the food sequence that follows. | terra: أَنَّا صَبَبْنَا ٱلْمَآءَ صَبًّا makes the poured rain the first explicit stage in the Quran's close analysis of human food.

luna: The earth is split open after the rain, a concrete counterpart to the section's vegetation being brought out from soil. | terra: ثُمَّ شَقَقْنَا ٱلْأَرْضَ شَقًّا shows the earth split for emergence, making concrete the section's claim that growth is pulled out from a place.
luna: The next product is grain, specifying one form of the earth's growth. | terra: Grain is the first named growth from poured water and split earth, marking the concrete emergence stage.
luna: This continuation names grapes among the growth brought out of earth. | terra: Grapes and herbage continue the fresh plant abundance before the passage arrives at explicit fodder.
luna: The verse adds olives and date palms to the rain-fed plant sequence. | terra: Olive and palm extend the varieties drawn out of the cracked earth by rain.

luna: The sequence then names dense gardens, the cultivated abundance behind the food image. | terra: Dense gardens supply the lush dark-green visual pole immediately before fruit and pasture are named.

luna: The verse names fruit and أَبًّا; the latter is pasture or fodder, directly meeting the section's plant-and-grazing sense of مرعى. | terra: Fruit and أَبًّا, pasture or fodder, are the end products of the poured water and split earth, directly meeting المرعى's plant-and-feed sense.

luna: This closing verse calls the fruit and pasture provision for people and their livestock, making the pasture's grazing function explicit. | terra: The whole rain-to-growth sequence is provision for people and their livestock, completing pasture as a relation between plant, animal, and provider.
terra: The oath by the sky “of return” evokes returning rain from above, the repeated descent behind the pasture's emergence.
terra: The paired oath by the splitting earth supplies the cracked ground through which the hidden plant is brought out.

luna: The verse says the people of the Fire have only thorny ضَرِيع for food; this is a specific boundary to the section's pasture as grazing and provision. | terra: The people of the Fire have only a harsh dry plant for food, turning vegetation from life-giving pasture into part of punishment.

luna: The next verse says that food neither nourishes nor relieves hunger, contrasting the pasture's sustaining growth with the Fire's barren provision. | terra: That plant neither nourishes nor relieves hunger, a sharp reversal of the pasture and rain whose very names carry feeding and life.
terra: Earth brings out its burdens, a non-botanical but strongly concrete instance of إخراج from a containing place that clarifies how literally the section pictures grass being drawn from soil.
terra: The defeated army becomes like eaten straw, another human catastrophe rendered as plant refuse and thus a close thematic cousin of people made غثاء in 23:41.
